q: What is the difference between the JDK, the JRE and the JVM?
o: They are three names for the same Java installation
JVM runs bytecode; JRE adds libraries; JDK adds tools like `javac`
JDK runs programs; JRE compiles them; JVM stores the results
JVM is the compiler; JDK is the editor; JRE is the debugger
e:
Java source code (`.java`) is first compiled into bytecode (`.class` files). Bytecode is not for your processor: it is for a program called the JVM (Java Virtual Machine), which reads it and runs it.
The JRE (Java Runtime Environment) is the JVM plus the standard class libraries, enough to RUN Java programs.
The JDK (Java Development Kit) is the JRE plus tools to BUILD programs: the compiler `javac`, `jar`, debuggers. As a developer you install the JDK.
r: JDK = build + run. JRE = run. JVM = the engine that executes bytecode.
fa: JVM runs bytecode; JRE = JVM + standard libraries; JDK = JRE + developer tools such as the compiler (`javac`)

q: "Write once, run anywhere" in Java is possible mainly because:
o: Java code is translated to each OS's machine code on every edit
The compiler makes bytecode, and each OS has a JVM that runs it
Java programs only work on Windows, which hides the differences
Java has no operating system dependencies at all, so nothing is needed
e:
`javac` compiles your code to bytecode, a neutral instruction set. The same `.class` or `.jar` file can be copied to Windows, Linux or macOS.
Each platform has its own JVM that translates bytecode to what that computer understands.
So you compile once; the JVM handles the differences between machines.
r: Bytecode is portable; the JVM is platform-specific.
fa: The compiler produces bytecode, and each OS has its own JVM that can run the same bytecode

q: Which statement about `int` and `Integer` is correct?
o: They are the same type, written two different ways
`int` is a primitive and cannot be null; `Integer` is an object and can
`Integer` is always faster than `int` because it is an object
`int` can be a generic type argument, as in `List<int>`
e:
Java has 8 primitive types (`int`, `long`, `double`, `boolean`, `char`, `byte`, `short`, `float`). They hold a plain value and can never be null.
Each primitive has a wrapper class (`Integer`, `Long`, `Double`...) that is a real object. It can be null and can be used in collections and generics: `List<Integer>` works, `List<int>` does not.
Java converts between them automatically (autoboxing/unboxing). Unboxing a null `Integer` throws NullPointerException.
r: Primitive = raw value. Wrapper = object (can be null).
fa: `int` is a primitive (cannot be null); `Integer` is an object wrapper (can be null)

q: What does this print?
o: true true
true false
false true
false false
e:
For objects, `==` compares references: are both variables pointing to the exact same object in memory? `new String(...)` always creates a new object, so `a == b` is false.
`.equals()` compares the content. Both strings contain "hi", so it is true.
Rule: use `.equals()` to compare text and other objects; use `==` for primitives and for checking `null`.
r: == compares references, equals() compares content.

q: Why should you avoid `s += x` for building a long string inside a big loop?
o: It is a syntax error when used inside a loop body
Strings are immutable, so each `+=` copies the old text
It converts the string to lowercase on every pass
It only works with numbers, not with plain text
e:
A `String` in Java can never change after creation (it is immutable). `s += x` really means: create a new String with the old text plus x, and throw the old one away.
In a loop with thousands of iterations that means thousands of copies, which is slow and creates garbage.
`StringBuilder` keeps an internal buffer that grows, so you append without copying every time. Call `.toString()` at the end.
r: Many appends in a loop: use StringBuilder.
fa: Strings are immutable, so each `+=` creates a brand new String, copying all previous characters

q: What does the keyword `static` mean on a method or field?
o: It cannot be changed after its first assignment
It belongs to the class, so no instance is needed
It is only visible inside the same source file
It runs automatically when the program starts up
e:
Normal (instance) fields and methods belong to each object: every `new Person()` has its own `name`.
A `static` member belongs to the class: there is only one copy, shared by all objects, and you call it as `ClassName.method()` without `new`. `Math.max(1, 2)` and `main` are static.
Careful: static mutable fields are shared state, which is a classic source of bugs in multi-threaded programs.
r: static = one copy per class, not per object.
fa: It belongs to the class itself, not to any single object, and you can use it without creating an instance

q: What does `final` do?
o: Variable: assign once. Method: no override. Class: no extends
It deletes the object at the end of the method call
It makes a variable global, so every class can change it
It marks the last line that the program will ever run
e:
`final` means "cannot be changed or replaced", and it applies differently:
- final variable: assigned once. For an object, the reference cannot point elsewhere, but the object's inside can still change (a `final List` can still receive `add`).
- final method: subclasses cannot override it.
- final class: nobody can extend it (`String` is final).
r: final = no reassign, no override, no extend.
fa: On a variable: it can be assigned only once. On a method: it cannot be overridden. On a class: it cannot be extended

q: Which access modifier is used when you write NO keyword in front of a field or method?
o: `public`: visible to every class in the project
`private`: visible only inside the same class
Package-private: visible only to classes in the same package
`protected`: visible to subclasses and the same package
e:
Java has four levels of visibility:
- `public`: everyone.
- `protected`: same package plus subclasses.
- (no keyword) package-private: only classes in the same package.
- `private`: only inside the same class.
Good practice (encapsulation): make fields `private` and expose only what is needed through public methods.
r: No keyword = package-private.

q: What is the main difference between an interface and an abstract class in Java?
o: There is no real difference, as both define methods
A class implements many interfaces but extends one class
Interfaces can have instance fields; abstract classes cannot
Abstract classes cannot contain any method with code
e:
An interface is a contract: a list of methods a class promises to provide (`implements`). A class can implement as many interfaces as it wants.
An abstract class is a half-built class that can have fields, constructors and some ready methods plus some `abstract` methods to complete. A class can `extend` only ONE class.
Since Java 8 interfaces can also have `default` methods with code, but they still cannot keep per-object state.
r: Many interfaces, one parent class. Only abstract classes carry state.
fa: A class can implement many interfaces but extend only one class; an abstract class can hold state (fields) and constructors

q: Which collection should you choose to store unique items with no duplicates?
o: `List`
`Set`
`Map` with duplicate keys
`Queue`
e:
The Collections Framework gives you ready-made data structures:
- `List`: ordered, allows duplicates, access by position (`ArrayList`).
- `Set`: no duplicates (`HashSet`, `TreeSet`).
- `Map`: key to value pairs, unique keys (`HashMap`).
- `Queue` / `Deque`: items processed in order (`ArrayDeque`).
Adding an existing item to a `Set` simply does nothing.
r: List = ordered with duplicates. Set = unique. Map = key to value.

q: In practice, which is the better default for a general-purpose list: `ArrayList` or `LinkedList`?
o: `LinkedList`, because it is always faster for every operation
`ArrayList`: fast index access and compact in memory
They behave exactly the same in speed and memory
`LinkedList`, because it is thread-safe and `ArrayList` is not
e:
`ArrayList` stores items in a resizable array: `get(i)` is instant (O(1)), appending is fast, and items sit together in memory, which CPUs like.
`LinkedList` stores each item in a separate node with links. Insertion in the middle is only cheap if you already hold the position; finding it takes O(n), and each node costs extra memory.
Use `ArrayList` by default, and `ArrayDeque` when you need a queue or stack.
r: Default to ArrayList.
fa: `ArrayList`: fast access by index and compact in memory; `LinkedList` is rarely better

q: Which of these is a CHECKED exception?
o: `NullPointerException`
`IllegalArgumentException`
`IOException`
`ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException`
e:
Checked exceptions extend `Exception` (but not `RuntimeException`). The compiler FORCES you to either catch them or declare them with `throws`. `IOException` (files, network) is the classic one.
Unchecked exceptions extend `RuntimeException` (NullPointerException, IllegalArgumentException, IndexOutOfBounds...). They usually mean a bug in the code, and the compiler does not force you to handle them.
`Error` (like OutOfMemoryError) is for serious JVM problems; you normally do not catch it.
r: Checked = compiler forces you to handle. Unchecked = RuntimeException.

q: What is the difference between method overloading and overriding?
o: Overload: same name, new params. Override: subclass replaces
They are just two names for the very same feature
Overloading needs inheritance; overriding works in one class
Overriding changes the parameters; overloading the return type
e:
Overloading: several methods with the same name but different parameter lists, e.g. `print(int)` and `print(String)`. The compiler picks the one that matches at compile time.
Overriding: a subclass provides its own version of an inherited method with the same name and parameters, usually with `@Override`. The JVM chooses at runtime based on the real object type (polymorphism).
r: Overload = same name, different params. Override = replace in a subclass.
fa: Overloading: same name, different parameters in the same class. Overriding: a subclass replaces a parent's method with the same signature

q: If you override `equals()` in a class, what else must you override, and why?
o: `toString()`, so that the object prints in a readable way
`hashCode()`, since equal objects must have the same hash code
`clone()`, so that equal objects can also be copied
Nothing else, because `equals()` works on its own
e:
The contract is: if `a.equals(b)` is true, then `a.hashCode() == b.hashCode()` must be true.
`HashMap` and `HashSet` first use the hash code to choose a bucket (a storage slot), and only then call `equals` inside that bucket. If two equal objects have different hash codes, they land in different buckets and the map will not find one when you search with the other.
Compute `hashCode` from the same fields you use in `equals` (`Objects.hash(a, b)`), or use a `record`.
r: Override equals => override hashCode with the same fields.
fa: `hashCode()`, because equal objects must return the same hash code or HashMap/HashSet will misbehave

q: What does this print?
o: true true
true false
false false
false true
e:
When you write `Integer a = 127`, Java does autoboxing: it calls `Integer.valueOf(127)`. To save memory, `valueOf` keeps a cache of Integer objects for -128 to 127 and reuses them.
So 127 gives the same object both times (`==` true), but 128 creates two different objects (`==` false).
Lesson: never compare wrapper objects with `==`; use `.equals()`.
r: Integer cache covers -128..127: compare wrappers with equals().

q: What is `try-with-resources` for?
o: Trying several resources in parallel until one works
Closing resources automatically, even after an error
Retrying an operation again and again until it succeeds
Allocating extra memory to the resource when needed
e:
Resources such as files, database connections and sockets must be closed or they leak. The old way needed a `finally` block with extra try/catch.
With `try (Resource r = ...) { ... }`, Java calls `r.close()` automatically when the block ends, normally or by exception. The resource must implement `AutoCloseable`. Resources close in reverse order of creation.
r: Open it in the try parentheses and Java closes it for you.
fa: Automatically closing resources (files, connections) at the end of the block, even if an exception happens

q: What is type erasure in Java generics?
o: Generics are erased at runtime, so `List<String>` is `List`
Generic types are erased from the source code after compiling
Java deletes any generic class that nobody uses anywhere
Generics make the program slower, as types are checked later
e:
Generics (`List<String>`) let the compiler check types so you do not need casts. After checking, the compiler removes (erases) the type arguments and keeps only the raw type in the bytecode.
Consequences: you cannot write `new T()`, `instanceof List<String>`, or create `new T[10]`, and `List<int>` is not allowed because type arguments must be objects.
r: Generics are a compile-time check only.
fa: Generic type information is removed by the compiler; at runtime a `List<String>` and a `List<Integer>` are both just `List`

q: What does this print?
o: [Ana, Alicia]
[ANA, ALICIA]
[ANA, BOB, ALICIA, CARL]
[A, A]
e:
A Stream is a pipeline for processing a collection: source, then intermediate steps, then a final (terminal) step.
`filter` keeps names starting with "A" (Ana, Alicia). `map(String::toUpperCase)` converts each to upper case. `toList()` collects the result.
The original list is not modified. `n -> n.startsWith("A")` is a lambda: a short anonymous function.
r: Stream = source, intermediate ops (filter/map), terminal op (toList/collect).

q: What does this print?
o: a1 a2 a3 done
done
done a1 a2 a3
Compile error
e:
Streams are lazy: the intermediate operations (`peek`, `map`, `filter`) only describe what to do. Nothing runs until a terminal operation (`collect`, `forEach`, `count`, `toList`...) is called.
Here there is no terminal operation, so the pipeline never runs and only "done" is printed.
r: No terminal operation = nothing executes.

q: What is the recommended way to use `Optional<T>`?
o: Call `optional.get()` directly each time you need a value
Return type for 'maybe absent', with `orElse` or `map`
Use it for each field and each method parameter, always
Use it as a way to make a class thread-safe in Java
e:
`Optional<T>` is a box that may or may not contain a value. It makes "this can be missing" visible in the method signature, instead of returning null and hoping callers remember to check.
Good use: `repo.findById(id).map(User::getName).orElse("unknown")` or `.orElseThrow()`.
Bad use: calling `.get()` without checking (it throws if empty), or using Optional for fields and parameters.
r: Optional is for return values; avoid bare get().
fa: Use it as a return type for "might be absent", and use `orElse`, `orElseThrow`, `map` instead of `get()` without checking

q: What do records (Java 16+) give you with `record Point(int x, int y) {}`?
o: A mutable class with setters for each component field
An immutable class with getters, `equals` and `toString`
A database table that is mapped from the components
A class that is not allowed to declare any methods
e:
A record is a short way to declare a plain data carrier. The compiler generates the constructor, accessors (`p.x()`, not `getX()`), `equals`, `hashCode` and `toString` from the listed components.
Fields are final, so records are immutable. They are ideal for DTOs, API responses and map keys. Records can still have extra methods and validation in a compact constructor.
r: record = immutable data class with boilerplate generated.
fa: An immutable data class with constructor, getters (`x()`), `equals`, `hashCode` and `toString` generated automatically

q: Where do objects live in the JVM, and what lives on the stack?
o: Objects on the stack; local primitives on the heap
Objects on the heap; each thread's stack holds locals and calls
Everything lives on the heap, including method calls
Everything lives on the stack, including all objects
e:
The heap is the big shared memory area where all objects are created (`new`). The garbage collector cleans it.
Each thread has its own stack: a small area where each method call gets a frame with its local variables (primitives and references to objects). When the method returns, the frame is removed automatically.
A `StackOverflowError` means too many nested calls (usually infinite recursion); `OutOfMemoryError` means the heap is full.
r: Heap = objects (shared). Stack = method frames (per thread).
fa: Objects on the heap; each thread's stack holds local variables and method calls

q: What does this print?
o: finally, then 1
1, then finally
finally only
e:
A `finally` block runs always, even if the `try` block executes `return`. Java first evaluates the return value (1), then runs `finally` (printing "finally"), then returns 1 to the caller.
So the output is `finally` on one line and `1` on the next.
Do not put `return` inside `finally`: it would replace the original result and even hide exceptions.
r: finally always runs, even after return.

q: Why does this code throw `ConcurrentModificationException`?
o: `remove` is not allowed on lists created with `new ArrayList`
The list was modified while the for-each iterator was walking it
`Integer` objects cannot be removed from a list
Another thread is changing the list at the same time
e:
The for-each loop uses an iterator behind the scenes. The iterator remembers how many modifications the list had when it started. If you add or remove through the list itself during the loop, the iterator notices the count changed and fails fast with this exception. It happens even with a single thread.
Safe options: `nums.removeIf(n -> n % 2 == 0)`, use `iterator.remove()`, or build a new list with a stream.
r: Do not modify a collection while iterating it; use removeIf or Iterator.remove.
fa: Because the list was structurally modified while the for-each iterator was walking it

q: Which is true about `HashMap`, `Hashtable` and `ConcurrentHashMap`?
o: All three are equally safe and fast when many threads use them
`HashMap` is unsafe; `Hashtable` locks all; `ConcurrentHashMap` is finer
`HashMap` is the only one that allows null keys, and it is thread-safe
`ConcurrentHashMap` is always slower than `Hashtable` in every case
e:
`HashMap` is fast but unsafe if several threads modify it at the same time (lost updates, even infinite loops in old versions).
`Hashtable` is synchronized on every method, so only one thread works at a time. It is legacy; avoid it.
`ConcurrentHashMap` is designed for concurrency: reads do not block and writes lock only small parts. It also offers atomic operations like `computeIfAbsent` and `merge`. It does not allow null keys or values.
r: Shared map between threads: ConcurrentHashMap.
fa: `HashMap` is not thread-safe; `Hashtable` locks the whole map (old, slow); `ConcurrentHashMap` allows many threads with fine-grained locking

q: What is the difference between `synchronized` and `volatile`?
o: They are identical in effect, only the keyword is different
`synchronized` locks and shares writes; `volatile` only shares
`volatile` locks the whole object; `synchronized` does not lock
`volatile` can only be applied to methods and never to fields
e:
`synchronized` makes a block run by one thread at a time (mutual exclusion) and also makes changes visible to the next thread that enters.
`volatile` on a field only guarantees visibility: when one thread writes, others immediately see the new value (no stale cached copy). It does NOT make `count++` safe, because that is three steps: read, add, write.
Use `volatile` for simple flags (`running = false`), `synchronized` or `AtomicInteger` for counters and compound actions.
r: volatile = visibility only. synchronized = lock + visibility.
fa: `synchronized` gives mutual exclusion plus visibility; `volatile` only guarantees that reads see the latest write (no atomicity for compound actions)

q: Why use an `ExecutorService` (thread pool) instead of `new Thread()` for every task?
o: Threads cannot be created with the `new` keyword at all
Threads are costly; a pool reuses a few and queues the rest
Executors make the code run on the GPU instead of the CPU
A pool guarantees that tasks never fail or throw exceptions
e:
Each thread uses memory (around 1 MB of stack) and the OS needs time to create it. If a server started a new thread per request, a traffic spike could create thousands and crash.
An `ExecutorService` keeps a limited set of worker threads that take tasks from a queue and are reused. You submit tasks and get a `Future` for the result. Always shut it down (`shutdown()`) when finished.
r: Thread pool = reuse a bounded set of threads.
fa: Creating threads is expensive and unlimited threads can exhaust memory; a pool reuses a fixed number of threads and queues extra tasks

q: When would you use `Comparator` instead of `Comparable`?
o: `Comparable` is for sorting; `Comparator` is for hashing
`Comparable` is the natural order; `Comparator` is external
They are identical, only the name of the method changes
`Comparator` only works on numbers and never on objects
e:
`Comparable<T>` is implemented by the class itself with `compareTo`. It defines ONE natural order (e.g. `String` alphabetical, `Integer` numeric).
`Comparator<T>` is a separate object with `compare(a, b)`. You can have many: by name, by age, by date. It is also the only choice when you cannot modify the class.
Modern style: `people.sort(Comparator.comparing(Person::getAge).thenComparing(Person::getName))`.
r: Comparable = natural order inside. Comparator = custom orders outside.
fa: `Comparable` defines the natural order inside the class; `Comparator` defines extra or external orderings without changing the class

q: Java has a garbage collector. How can a Java program still have a memory leak?
o: It cannot, because the GC always frees every object
By keeping references to objects it no longer needs
Only by calling `System.gc()` too many times in a row
Only by using primitives instead of objects everywhere
e:
The GC frees objects that nothing can reach anymore. A leak in Java means objects are still reachable (something still points to them) but your program will never use them again.
Typical causes: a static `Map` used as a cache with no size limit or expiry; listeners or callbacks registered and never removed; `ThreadLocal` values in pooled threads; unclosed resources.
Symptoms: heap grows until `OutOfMemoryError`. Tools: heap dump + Eclipse MAT, VisualVM, JFR.
r: Leak = still reachable but never used again.
fa: By keeping references to objects that are no longer needed, e.g. a static map/cache that only grows, forgotten listeners, or unclosed ThreadLocals

q: What problem do virtual threads (Java 21) solve?
o: They make CPU-heavy code run faster on more cores
Simple blocking code scaled to huge numbers of tasks
They replace the garbage collector with a cheaper one
They remove the need for synchronization in shared code
e:
A normal (platform) thread maps 1:1 to an OS thread and is expensive, so a server can only have a few thousand. When a thread waits for I/O (database, HTTP), it just sits there wasting its slot.
Virtual threads are lightweight threads managed by the JVM. When one blocks on I/O, the JVM parks it and runs another on the same OS thread. You can create millions.
They help with I/O-bound workloads (typical web services). They do NOT speed up CPU-bound work, and you still need to protect shared data.
r: Virtual threads = cheap blocking for I/O-heavy servers.
fa: They let you write simple blocking code while handling hundreds of thousands of concurrent tasks, because they are very cheap and the JVM, not the OS, schedules them

q: Why is this counter NOT thread-safe even though the field is `volatile`?
o: `volatile` only works on object references, not on `int` fields
`count++` is read, add, write: two threads can read the same value
An `int` field cannot be shared between threads
It is thread-safe, because `volatile` covers every operation
e:
`volatile` guarantees that every thread sees the latest written value. But `count++` is not one step: (1) read count, (2) add 1, (3) write back.
If two threads both read 5, both write 6, and one increment is lost (a race condition).
Fixes: `AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet()` (lock-free and atomic), or make the method `synchronized`, or use `LongAdder` for very high contention.
r: volatile does not make compound operations atomic.
fa: Because `count++` is read, add, write: two threads can read the same value and one update is lost

q: What is the practical difference between `thenApply` and `thenCompose` in `CompletableFuture`?
o: There is no difference at all, both are the same method
`thenApply` maps a result; `thenCompose` flattens futures
`thenCompose` blocks the thread; `thenApply` does not
`thenApply` handles the errors; `thenCompose` does not
e:
A `CompletableFuture<T>` represents a result that will exist later, without blocking while you wait.
`thenApply(f)`: when the result arrives, apply a plain function `T -> U` and get a `CompletableFuture<U>`.
`thenCompose(f)`: use when `f` itself returns a `CompletableFuture<U>` (for example, another async call). Without it you would get a nested `CompletableFuture<CompletableFuture<U>>`.
It is the same idea as `map` vs `flatMap`.
ec:
CompletableFuture<Order> order =
    findUserAsync(id)                       // CF<User>
        .thenCompose(u -> findOrderAsync(u)) // CF<Order>
        .thenApply(o -> o.withTax());
r: thenApply = map. thenCompose = flatMap.
fa: `thenApply` transforms the result with a normal function; `thenCompose` is for a function that itself returns a CompletableFuture and flattens it (like flatMap)

q: How do you make a class truly immutable in Java?
o: Mark only the class as `final`; nothing more is needed
`final` class, private final fields, no setters, copies
Add `volatile` to every one of the fields in the class
Make every field `static` so that all objects share it
e:
An immutable object never changes after construction, so it is automatically thread-safe and can be shared and cached freely (`String` and `LocalDate` are immutable).
Recipe: (1) `final` class so nobody subclasses and adds mutability, (2) `private final` fields, (3) no setters, (4) if a field is a mutable object (a `List`, a `Date`), copy it in the constructor and return a copy or an unmodifiable view in the getter.
A `final List` field alone is not enough: the list contents could still change. Records do most of this for you (but still need defensive copies of mutable components).
r: final fields + no setters + defensive copies.
fa: Make the class final, all fields `private final`, no setters, and defensively copy any mutable object that comes in or goes out

q: A class overrides `equals` but NOT `hashCode`. What is the likely result?
o: Always 1, because equal objects always share one slot
Likely 2: default hashCodes differ, so different buckets
Always 0, since the set rejects objects with no hashCode
A compile error, because `hashCode` is mandatory in Java
e:
Without an override, `hashCode()` comes from `Object` and is based on the object's identity, so two different `P` objects almost always get different hash codes.
`HashSet` uses the hash to pick a bucket. The two objects go to different buckets, so `equals` is never compared, and both are stored: size 2, even though `equals` says they are the same.
This breaks the contract. Fix: also override `hashCode` with `Objects.hash(n)`.
r: Broken equals/hashCode contract = duplicates in hash collections.
fa: Most likely 2: the default hashCode differs per object, so they land in different buckets and equals is never even called

q: What does a "stop-the-world" pause in garbage collection mean, and how do modern collectors reduce it?
o: The program is stopped forever and has to be restarted
All app threads pause during GC; G1 and ZGC shorten it
The GC stops the operating system for a short time
It only happens when `System.gc()` is called by hand
e:
To safely move or free objects, the GC sometimes needs every application thread to pause. That pause is called stop-the-world. Long pauses make a service freeze (high latency spikes).
G1 (default since Java 9) splits the heap into regions and collects the ones with most garbage first, aiming at a target pause time.
ZGC and Shenandoah do almost all work concurrently, with pauses of about a millisecond, even on very large heaps.
Tuning starts by measuring: GC logs (`-Xlog:gc`), not by guessing flags.
r: Pause = threads frozen for GC. G1/ZGC aim for short pauses.
fa: All application threads are paused while the GC works; collectors like G1 and ZGC do most work concurrently or in small regions to keep pauses short

q: Explain the four pillars of OOP with Java examples.
a:
- Encapsulation: hide data (`private` fields) and expose behavior through methods, so the class controls its own rules.
- Inheritance: a class reuses and extends another (`class Dog extends Animal`). Prefer composition when it is not a true "is-a".
- Polymorphism: the same call behaves differently depending on the real object: `Animal a = new Dog(); a.speak();` runs Dog's version.
- Abstraction: expose what something does, hide how: interfaces and abstract classes (`List` vs `ArrayList`).
- Interview tip: give one tiny example for each and say when inheritance is a bad idea.

q: Explain how a HashMap works internally.
a:
- It keeps an array of buckets. For `put(key, value)` it computes `key.hashCode()`, spreads the bits, and picks `index = hash % arraySize`.
- If the bucket is empty, the entry is stored. If not (a collision), entries are chained in a linked list; since Java 8, a long chain (8+) becomes a balanced tree for faster search.
- `get(key)`: find the bucket by hash, then use `equals` to find the exact key. That is why `equals` and `hashCode` must be consistent.
- When the map is more than 75% full (load factor 0.75), the array doubles and entries are redistributed (rehash).
- Average O(1) get and put, worst case O(log n). Not thread-safe; allows one null key.

q: Explain the Java memory model: heap, stack, metaspace and garbage collection.
a:
- Heap: where all objects live; shared by all threads; divided into young generation (new objects, collected often and cheaply) and old generation (survivors, collected less often).
- Stack: one per thread; holds method frames with local variables and references.
- Metaspace: class definitions and metadata (outside the heap, grows with native memory).
- GC: finds objects no longer reachable from roots (stack variables, static fields) and frees them. Common collectors: G1 (default), ZGC, Parallel.
- Common errors: `OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space` (heap full or leak), `StackOverflowError` (deep or infinite recursion).

q: What concurrency tools does Java give you, and when do you use each?
a:
- `synchronized` / `ReentrantLock`: protect shared mutable state with mutual exclusion.
- `volatile`: visibility of a simple flag.
- `Atomic*` / `LongAdder`: lock-free counters.
- `ConcurrentHashMap`, `CopyOnWriteArrayList`, `BlockingQueue`: thread-safe collections for shared data and producer/consumer.
- `ExecutorService`: thread pools to run tasks; `CompletableFuture`: compose async steps.
- Virtual threads (Java 21): simple blocking style for massive I/O concurrency.
- Best rule: avoid shared mutable state; prefer immutable objects and message passing.

q: What changed in modern Java (8 to 21) that every developer should know?
a:
- Java 8: lambdas, streams, `Optional`, `default` methods, `java.time` API.
- Java 9 to 11: modules, `var` for local variables, `List.of`, HTTP client; Java 11 is an LTS (long-term support).
- Java 14 to 17: records, switch expressions, text blocks, sealed classes, pattern matching for `instanceof`; Java 17 is an LTS.
- Java 21 (LTS): virtual threads, record patterns, pattern matching for `switch`, sequenced collections.
- Say: "I mainly target the current LTS and use records, streams and `Optional` daily."

q: What is Java?
o: A general-purpose, object-oriented language for backends
A markup language used to describe the layout of web pages
A database engine used to store and query structured data
A web browser used to open sites and run page scripts
e:
Java is a programming language. Programs are made of classes, and the same compiled program can run on Windows, Linux or macOS because it runs on the Java Virtual Machine.
It is very common in banks, large companies, backend services and Android history. Frameworks such as Spring Boot make it popular for web backends.
Java is NOT JavaScript.
r: Java = object-oriented language that runs on the JVM.
fa: A general-purpose, object-oriented programming language widely used for backend and enterprise software

q: What happens between writing Java code and running it?
o: `javac` makes `.class` bytecode; `java` runs it on the JVM
The browser reads the `.java` file and runs it directly
The code is converted into JavaScript and executed there
Nothing: the CPU runs the `.java` text exactly as written
e:
The Java tutorial describes the steps:
1. You write source code in plain text files ending in `.java`.
2. The compiler `javac` turns them into `.class` files. They contain bytecode, the machine language of the Java Virtual Machine, not code for your CPU.
3. The `java` tool runs your application with an instance of the JVM.
Maven and your IDE do these steps for you, but this is what happens underneath.
ec:
javac Hello.java   # creates Hello.class (bytecode)
java Hello         # JVM runs the bytecode
r: .java → javac → .class (bytecode) → JVM runs it.
fa: `javac` compiles the `.java` files into `.class` files of bytecode, then the `java` launcher runs them on the JVM

q: What is the JVM (Java Virtual Machine)?
o: A program that runs bytecode between your code and the OS
An editor that writes and checks the Java source code
A cloud server that hosts Java applications for you
A database that stores Java objects between the runs
e:
Bytecode is not tied to a specific processor or operating system. Each operating system has its own JVM that knows how to run it.
This is the idea behind 'write once, run anywhere'.
The JVM also manages memory for you: it creates objects and the garbage collector removes the ones no longer used.
r: JVM = the engine that runs Java bytecode on any OS.
fa: A program that runs Java bytecode and sits between your program and the operating system, so the same `.class` files run on Windows, Linux or macOS

q: What do you install to write, compile and run Java programs?
o: A JDK (Java Development Kit)
Only a web browser with a Java plugin
Only Maven, which downloads the rest
Only a JavaScript runtime such as Node
e:
The JDK includes the compiler (`javac`), the runtime with the JVM and other tools.
Older Java versions also had a JRE (Java Runtime Environment), a package with only what is needed to run programs. Since JDK 11 Oracle offers only the JDK, and smaller runtimes can be built with `jlink`.
Common JDK distributions: Oracle JDK, OpenJDK builds such as Eclipse Temurin.
r: JDK = everything to develop and run Java.

q: What does LTS mean for Java versions, and which versions are LTS?
o: Long-Term Support: Java 8, 11, 17, 21 and 25
Latest Test Snapshot: every odd-numbered version
Language Translation System: Java versions 1 to 5
Legacy Tools Suite: only Java 8 and older versions
e:
New Java versions come out regularly, but only some are Long-Term Support releases. Companies usually choose an LTS version for production.
Oracle's roadmap lists LTS releases: 8 (2014), 11 (2018), 17 (2021), 21 (2023) and 25 (September 2025). A new LTS is planned every two years.
When a job says 'Java 17 or 21', it means these LTS versions.
fa: Long-Term Support: versions that get updates for years; Java 8, 11, 17, 21 and 25 are LTS releases

q: In Java, what are a class and an object?
c:
Bicycle bike1 = new Bicycle();
Bicycle bike2 = new Bicycle();
o: A class is a blueprint; an object is an instance made with `new`
A class is a variable; an object is a file on disk
An object is the blueprint; a class is one instance of it
They are the same thing under two different names
e:
The Java tutorial: a class is the blueprint from which individual objects are created.
Here `Bicycle` is the class. `bike1` and `bike2` are two separate objects (instances), each with its own data: one can be at gear 2 while the other is at gear 3.
`new` creates a new object in memory.
r: Class = blueprint. Object = instance made with new.
fa: A class is a blueprint; an object is one instance created from it with `new`

q: In a Java class, what are fields and methods?
o: Fields store the object's state; methods define its behavior
Fields are functions; methods are variables
Fields run the program; methods are only comments
They are the same thing, just named differently
e:
The Java tutorial: an object stores its state in fields and exposes its behavior through methods.
Example: for a `Bicycle`, the fields are `speed` and `gear`; the methods are `speedUp()` and `changeGear()`.
Methods work on the object's fields. Keeping fields private and using methods to change them is called encapsulation.
r: Fields = data. Methods = actions.
fa: Fields store the object's state (data); methods define its behavior (actions)

q: What does this code do?
o: Declares an int holding 30 and a String holding Ana
Compares age with 30 and stores the result in name
Creates two new classes that are called age and name
Imports two packages that are called age and name
e:
Java is statically typed: every variable must have a declared type before you use it. `int` is a whole number, `String` is text, `double` a decimal number and `boolean` true or false.
A semicolon `;` ends each statement. Text goes in double quotes.
You cannot put text into an int variable: the compiler rejects it, which catches mistakes before running.
r: Java: declare the type, then the name, then the value.
fa: Declares two variables with their types: an int (whole number) holding 30 and a String (text) holding Ana

q: What is `public static void main(String[] args)`?
o: The entry point: the method the JVM calls to start
A required import that every Java file must contain
A database command that starts a new connection
A comment style that is used to document a class
e:
When you run `java Hello`, the JVM looks for a `main` method in that class and starts there.
- public: callable from outside the class.
- static: it belongs to the class, so no object is needed.
- void: it returns nothing.
- String[] args: the command-line arguments.
In Spring Boot, `main` is where `SpringApplication.run(...)` starts the app. JDK 25 also allows simpler forms such as `void main()` (JEP 512), but you will see the classic form almost everywhere.
r: main = where a Java program starts.
fa: The classic entry point: the method the JVM calls to start a Java program

q: What are a package and an `import` in Java?
o: A package groups classes; `import` allows short class names
A package is a delivery box; `import` deletes a class
A package is a database table; `import` creates one
Both are comment styles that are used to document code
e:
The Java tutorial: a package is a namespace that organizes a set of related classes and interfaces, like folders on a computer.
Example: `java.util.List` is the class `List` in the package `java.util`. After `import java.util.List;` you can write just `List`.
Your own code is organized in packages too, usually named after the company domain reversed, like `com.mycompany.shop`.
r: Package = folder-like namespace. import = use a class from it.
fa: A package is a namespace that groups related classes; `import` lets you use a class from another package by its short name

q: What is a JAR file?
o: A ZIP-based file that bundles classes and resources
A code editor that is installed together with the JDK
A type of exception thrown when a class is missing
A Maven command that cleans the whole project folder
e:
After compiling, you have many `.class` files. A JAR packs them into one file.
Libraries are distributed as JARs (for example Jackson or JUnit). A Spring Boot application is usually built as an executable JAR that you start with `java -jar app.jar`.
With Maven, `mvn package` puts the JAR in the `target` folder.
r: JAR = a zip of compiled Java code.
fa: A Java ARchive: a ZIP-based file that bundles compiled classes and resources so a library or application can be shipped as one file

q: What is a Java interface?
o: A contract: method signatures that a class promises to implement
A visual screen that users see in the application
A database connection that a class opens and closes
A kind of loop that repeats until a condition is false
e:
The Java tutorial: interfaces form a contract between the class and the outside world, enforced at build time by the compiler.
If a class says it implements an interface, all its methods must exist or the code will not compile.
Example: `interface Payment { void pay(int amount); }` can be implemented by `CardPayment` and `PayPalPayment`. Callers only need to know the interface.
r: Interface = a contract that classes implement.
fa: A contract: a group of method signatures that a class promises to implement; the compiler checks that it does

q: What does `null` mean in Java, and what is a NullPointerException?
o: `null` means no object is referenced; using it throws NullPointerException
`null` equals zero; the exception appears when dividing by zero
`null` is an empty string; the exception happens on empty strings
`null` is a keyword that marks the end of a loop
e:
A variable that holds an object really holds a reference (an address). `null` means 'no object'.
`String s = null; s.length();` crashes with NullPointerException (NPE), because there is no object to ask for its length.
Typical fixes: check for null, initialize variables, or use `Optional` to make 'maybe nothing' explicit.
r: null = no object. Using it as an object → NPE.
fa: `null` means a reference points to no object; calling a method on it throws a NullPointerException

q: What is an IDE?
o: Integrated Development Environment: an editor plus tools
A type of server that hosts and runs web applications
A programming language that is used to write compilers
A cloud service that builds and deploys the projects
e:
You can write code in any text editor, but an IDE saves a lot of time: it highlights errors as you type, suggests code, refactors safely, runs tests and lets you pause the program in a debugger.
IntelliJ IDEA and Eclipse are common for Java; PyCharm for Python. Editors such as VS Code become IDE-like with extensions.
r: IDE = editor + debugger + tools in one app.
fa: Integrated Development Environment: an editor with extra tools such as autocomplete, a debugger and run/test buttons, for example IntelliJ IDEA, Eclipse or PyCharm
